caption:
Meta made $64.6 billion in revenue last quarter, up 26% and above Wall Street's forecast.
But it spent $34.9 billion on AI data centers and chips, more than its business brought in, so free cash flow went negative.
To keep paying for the AI race, Meta is creating a new nonvoting Class C stock that keeps Zuckerberg in control.

Is Meta's AI bet worth burning cash for?

Follow @neurafeed.ai for daily AI news.

Source: Fortune · Photo: Roberto Schmidt / AFP via Getty Images

slides.headline: Meta made $64.6 billion in three months. Its *AI spending* still burned through all the cash

slides.heading: Revenue jumped *26%*
paras: Meta reported $64.6 billion in third quarter revenue on October 21, beating Wall Street's forecast.
Profit fell to $3.83 a share after a $9.89 billion charge for a settlement with 52 state attorneys general.

slides.heading: *$34.9 billion* in one quarter
paras: Meta spent $34.91 billion on capital expenses as it builds AI data centers. Its operations brought in $32.79 billion.

paras.t: Free cash flow turned negative: minus $2.12 billion.

slides.heading: A new stock with *no vote*
paras: Meta is creating a nonvoting Class C stock. Every Class A and Class B share gets one Class C share, effective January 19, 2027.
Meta says it can use them to raise money, pay staff and buy companies.

slides.heading: Up to *$145 billion* this year
paras: Meta now expects $135 billion to $145 billion in 2026 capital spending and says it will keep investing aggressively in 2027.
Zuckerberg told analysts he expects Muse to be "highly profitable."

slides.hook: Meta is betting its cash on AI. Follow to see if Muse pays it back.

site_article.headline: Meta revenue rises 26% as AI spending pushes free cash flow below zero
site_article.dek: Meta reported $64.6 billion in third quarter revenue and announced a nonvoting Class C stock that it says can help fund growth.
site_article.summary: Meta reported third quarter 2026 revenue of $64.6 billion, up 26% from a year earlier, while capital spending of $34.91 billion pushed free cash flow to minus $2.12 billion. The company also approved a nonvoting Class C stock that takes effect on January 19, 2027.
site_article.seo_title: Meta Q3 2026: revenue up 26%, AI spending turns cash flow negative
site_article.seo_description: Meta posted $64.6 billion in Q3 revenue, spent $34.9 billion on capital expenses and announced nonvoting Class C shares.
site_article.answer_summary: Meta earned $64.6 billion in revenue in the third quarter of 2026, but capital spending on AI infrastructure exceeded its operating cash flow, leaving free cash flow at minus $2.12 billion.
site_article.hero_alt: A man in a dark suit and red tie, photographed at a public event.

paragraphs.text: Meta reported third quarter 2026 revenue of $64.6 billion on October 21, an increase of 26% from a year earlier. Analysts had expected about $63.3 billion, according to Fortune, which cited Visible Alpha consensus data.

Net income came to $9.86 billion, or $3.83 per diluted share, compared with $1.05 per share a year earlier, when results were weighed down by a large one-time tax charge. The latest quarter included a $9.89 billion charge tied to an agreement with 52 state attorneys general. Excluding that charge, Meta said, operating income would have been $22.88 billion and earnings $7.40 per share.

Capital expenditures, including finance lease principal payments, reached $34.91 billion in the quarter, up from $19.37 billion a year earlier. Cash from operations was $32.79 billion, which left free cash flow at minus $2.12 billion, compared with $10.63 billion in the same quarter of 2025, according to the company's figures as reported by StockTitan.

Meta narrowed its full year 2026 capital spending forecast to between $135 billion and $145 billion, raising the low end from $130 billion. Seoul Economic Daily reported that the higher floor reflects heavier than expected spending on data center computing. Meta gave no figure for 2027 but said it expects to keep investing aggressively in its core business and its AI projects.

Operating margin fell to 20% from 40% a year earlier, and headcount stood at 66,775 at the end of the quarter, down 15%. Reality Labs, the unit behind Meta's headsets and glasses, lost $4.13 billion in the quarter.

Meta's board approved a publicly listed Class C common stock that carries no voting rights. Holders of Class A and Class B shares will receive one Class C share for each share they own, once a charter amendment takes effect on January 19, 2027. Meta expects the Class A share price to reflect a two for one split after the distribution and plans to list the new shares on Nasdaq.

The company said the new stock could be used for raising capital, employee compensation and acquisitions, and that it would help sustain the founder led model under Mark Zuckerberg. Crypto Briefing reported that Zuckerberg holds about 61% of the voting power.

Shares rose more than 3% in trading after the report, according to Forbes and Seoul Economic Daily. Forbes reported that Zuckerberg told analysts he expects the Muse AI agent to be highly profitable. Meta guided fourth quarter revenue to between $73 billion and $76 billion.

The quarter shows the tension in Meta's strategy. Its advertising business is still growing quickly, but the buildout of AI data centers now costs more each quarter than the company generates in operating cash. The nonvoting shares give Meta a new way to raise money and pay for acquisitions without weakening Zuckerberg's control.
The next signal is Meta's 2027 budget, which the company said it is still developing, and whether Muse begins to produce revenue that offsets the spending.
